Optimisation — a reproducible note
A reproducible technical note

Optimisation, from First Principles to Deep Learning

Gradient descent to natural gradients — how every modern model is actually trained, built from the calculus and linear algebra you already know
Dr. Dipak Munshi  ·  ML & Statistics Notes  ·  basic to advanced, with pen-and-paper derivations and computed examples

Almost everything in computational science and machine learning, underneath, is a minimisation. Fitting a model is minimising a loss. Training a neural network is minimising a loss. Maximum likelihood is minimising a negative log-likelihood; a Bayesian posterior is found by maximising, or by exploring, the same surface. Calibration, control, portfolio construction, experiment design — all of it reduces to find the input that makes this number as small as possible. This note is about how that is actually done.

The surprising thing, once you have seen it, is how few ideas do all the work, and how they recur. Follow the slope downhill. When the slope alone is slow, use curvature — how the slope is itself changing — to take a smarter step. When the surface is too large or too noisy to measure the slope exactly, use a cheap, random estimate of it and take many small steps. When different directions have wildly different scales, rescale them. That is, more or less, the whole subject: gradient descent, second-order methods, stochastic methods, and preconditioning. Everything else is these four ideas, sharpened for a particular setting.

The note runs from the ground up to the methods that train today's largest models, and it is deliberately one continuous story rather than a catalogue. We start with what an optimisation problem is and when we can hope to solve it (convexity), then build gradient descent and understand exactly why it is slow when it is slow (the condition number). We add momentum, then the second-order machinery — Newton, quasi-Newton (BFGS, L-BFGS), and the Gauss–Newton and Levenberg–Marquardt methods that dominate least-squares fitting. One chapter is devoted to the three curvature matrices — the Hessian, the Gauss–Newton matrix and the Fisher information — because understanding how they relate is the key that unlocks natural-gradient and modern second-order optimisers, and because the same Fisher matrix is the object a physicist already knows from parameter forecasting. We then turn to convex and constrained optimisation (Lagrange multipliers and the KKT conditions), and finally to the stochastic world: SGD, the adaptive family (AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam), natural gradient and K-FAC, the newest second-order methods for deep learning (Shampoo, SOAP), the practical craft of training large models, and the global and derivative-free methods — including Bayesian optimisation — for when you cannot differentiate at all.

How to read this

Every chapter has the derivation done properly once, a small pen-and-paper example you can follow with a pencil, and a computed figure showing the method at work — every number and curve regenerated from the algorithm in the text, nothing cited. The appendix collects the load-bearing lines of code. You can read it front to back, or drop into a chapter: each is self-contained, with pointers back to the one idea it builds on. A reader comfortable with vector calculus and linear algebra has everything needed; a reader who only wants the practical deep-learning methods can start at Chapter 11 and refer back.

A note on notation. We minimise a scalar objective over a vector of parameters ; the gradient is (the vector of first derivatives) and the Hessian is (the matrix of second derivatives). A superscript star, , marks an optimum. In the machine-learning chapters the parameters are usually called or and the objective is a loss averaged over data; nothing changes but the letters. Minimising and maximising are the same problem, so everything said about minimisation applies, with a sign flip, to maximum-likelihood and maximum-a-posteriori estimation.

1The optimisation problem

What we are looking for, how we recognise it when we find it, and the one property — convexity — that separates problems we can solve with confidence from problems we can only make progress on.

The problem is to find where is a scalar objective (also called the cost, loss, or energy). Sometimes is free to be anything in (unconstrained); sometimes it must satisfy equalities or inequalities (constrained), which we take up in Chapter 10. The value is the minimum; the location is the minimiser, and it is almost always the minimiser we want.

1.1  Local pictures: gradient and Hessian

Near any point , a smooth function looks like a quadratic. This is just Taylor's theorem, and it is the single most useful fact in optimisation: with the gradient and the Hessian. The gradient points in the direction of steepest increase, and its negative, , is the direction of steepest decrease — the first thing any descent method does is move along . The Hessian describes the curvature: how the slope bends as you move. Almost every method in this note is a different answer to one question: given the local quadratic picture, what step should I take?

Optimality conditions

At a local minimum of a smooth :

First order (necessary): . The slope is flat in every direction — a stationary point. This is the equation almost every method is secretly trying to solve.
Second order (sufficient): (necessary) and, with strictness (positive definite), sufficient. Curvature is upward in every direction, so you really are at the bottom of a bowl and not on a ridge or at a saddle.

A stationary point need not be a minimum. If is positive definite it is a minimum; negative definite, a maximum; and if has both positive and negative eigenvalues, a saddle — downhill in some directions, uphill in others. Saddles turn out to be the characteristic obstacle in high-dimensional non-convex problems like neural-network training, and we return to them in Chapter 16.

1.2  Convexity: the great divide

A set is convex if the straight line between any two of its points stays inside it. A function is convex if the chord between any two points on its graph lies on or above the graph: Equivalently, for smooth , convexity means the Hessian is positive semidefinite everywhere, — the function curves upward (or flat) in every direction at every point.

Why this one property matters so much: for a convex function, every local minimum is a global minimum, and any stationary point is a global minimum. Solving is then enough; there is nowhere worse to get stuck. This is the dividing line of the whole subject. Convex problems (linear and logistic regression, support-vector machines, LASSO, many control and portfolio problems) can be solved to provable global optimality, often fast. Non-convex problems (neural networks, most inverse problems, mixture models) have many local minima and saddles, and any method can only promise to find a good stationary point, not the best one. Remarkably, this weaker guarantee is often enough in practice — a theme of the machine-learning chapters.

Pen and paper: a one-line convexity check

Is convex? Compute the Hessian: . It is constant (so is quadratic). Check positive definiteness by its leading minors: the top-left entry is , and the determinant is . Both positive, so : the function is strictly convex, has exactly one minimum, and we will be able to find it with any method in the next few chapters. Had the determinant been negative, would have a negative eigenvalue and the only stationary point would be a saddle.

1.3  Conditioning: the hidden difficulty

Convexity says a minimum is findable; it does not say findable quickly. For a convex quadratic the speed is governed by the condition number , the ratio of the largest to smallest eigenvalue of the Hessian. Geometrically is how stretched the bowl is: is a perfectly round bowl, and large is a long narrow valley. A round bowl is trivial; a valley is where gradient descent struggles, because the gradient points across the valley rather than along it. The condition number is the number to watch for the rest of Part I, and defeating it — by momentum, by curvature, by preconditioning — is what most of the cleverness in optimisation is for.

2Gradient descent: the workhorse

The simplest method that works: repeatedly step downhill. Understanding exactly how fast it converges — and why a long narrow valley defeats it — explains almost every more sophisticated method that follows.

Gradient descent is one line: with the step size or learning rate. Each step moves in the direction of steepest descent, , by an amount . That is the entire algorithm; everything interesting is in choosing and in understanding how quickly the iterates approach .

2.1  Why the step size is a tightrope

Specialise to a quadratic with (the local picture near any minimum, by Taylor). The gradient is , so the step is . Diagonalise into its eigenvalues ; along each eigen-direction the error simply multiplies by each step: For convergence we need for every eigenvalue, i.e. . Too small and every direction crawls; too large and the stiffest direction (largest ) overshoots and diverges. The step size is a single scalar that must suit every direction at once — the tension that the whole subject exists to resolve.

Pen and paper: the optimal step and the rate

Take , so , , condition number . The error factor in direction is ; we want the worst of these as small as possible. The best balances the two extremes, , giving So at best the error shrinks by a factor per step — it takes about steps to gain six digits. For (a round bowl) the factor is : one step. All the slowness is the condition number.

2.2  Convergence rates, named

It is worth fixing the vocabulary, because the whole field is organised around it. A method converges linearly if the error shrinks by a constant factor each step, — a straight line on a log plot. Smaller is faster; gradient descent on a strongly convex problem is linear with . A method converges sublinearly if the factor itself drifts toward (e.g. error ); plain gradient descent on a merely convex (not strongly convex) problem is sublinear at . And a method converges quadratically if the number of correct digits roughly doubles each step, — this is the prize that Newton's method wins (Chapter 5), and nothing first-order can match it near the solution.

2.3  Choosing the step in practice

In real problems we do not know , and the objective is not globally quadratic. Three practical answers recur. Use a fixed step small enough to be stable, the default in deep learning where the curvature is unknown and changing. Use a decreasing schedule , essential once gradients are noisy (Chapter 11). Or use a line search that chooses afresh each step to guarantee sufficient decrease (Chapter 4) — the standard in classical deterministic optimisation. Which you pick is largely a question of whether you can afford to evaluate many times per step: cheap in a low-dimensional fit, far too expensive in a billion-parameter network.

3Momentum and acceleration

A memory of past steps lets gradient descent build speed along the valley while damping the zigzag across it — and, remarkably, achieves the best rate any first-order method can.

The zigzag of Chapter 2 happens because each gradient step forgets the last. Along the valley the gradients all point roughly the same way and should accumulate; across the valley they flip sign each step and should cancel. Momentum does exactly this by keeping a running velocity: with the momentum coefficient (typically ). The velocity is an exponentially-weighted average of past gradients; consistent directions reinforce, oscillating ones wash out. The physical picture is a heavy ball rolling down the surface with friction : it picks up speed on long gentle slopes and rolls through the small side-to-side wobbles.

3.1  How much momentum buys

On a quadratic, momentum changes the convergence rate from to . The square root is the whole point: for a valley with , plain gradient descent needs steps per digit while momentum needs . The improvement grows without bound as problems get more ill-conditioned, which is why momentum is not an optional tweak but a default.

Pen and paper: why past gradients add up

Unroll the velocity with constant gradient (a long straight valley): , , , and in the limit With the effective step along a consistent direction is times a single gradient step — the ball reaches a terminal velocity ten times faster than descent would crawl. In a direction where flips sign every step, the same geometric series largely cancels, so that direction is damped. One mechanism, opposite effects in the two kinds of direction: precisely what the valley needs.

3.2  Nesterov's accelerated gradient

A small change sharpens momentum into something provably optimal. Nesterov's method evaluates the gradient not at the current point but at the point momentum is about to carry you to: This “look-ahead” gradient acts as a correction: if the velocity is about to overshoot, the gradient at the look-ahead point already points back, braking earlier. For smooth convex functions Nesterov's method attains convergence, and Nesterov proved no method using only gradients can beat that order — it is the accelerated rate, the first-order speed limit. Momentum and its variants are thus not heuristics; they saturate a theorem.

The deep-learning caveat

Everything above is for a fixed, exact gradient. With the noisy stochastic gradients of neural-network training (Chapter 11) the clean and guarantees weaken, and momentum's role shifts: it mainly averages out gradient noise and helps roll through small barriers and saddles, rather than delivering textbook acceleration. It remains indispensable — the momentum term in Adam (Chapter 12) is this same velocity — but for averaging as much as for acceleration.

4Line search and trust regions

Two disciplined ways to decide how far to move once you have chosen a direction — the machinery that makes classical deterministic optimisation reliable rather than a matter of guessing the step size.

Every method so far picks a direction (for gradient descent, ) and then must decide how far to go. Fixing the step size by hand is fragile. The two robust alternatives — line search and trust regions — are the reason a routine like BFGS or Levenberg–Marquardt “just works” on a well-posed problem without babysitting.

4.1  Line search: choose the distance along the ray

Given a descent direction (one with , so initially decreases along it), a line search picks a step length to make a genuine improvement. We do not need the exact minimiser along the ray — that is wasteful — only a step that decreases “enough.” The Armijo (sufficient-decrease) condition asks that the actual decrease be at least a fraction of what the slope predicts: Backtracking is the simplest implementation: start with , and while Armijo fails, shrink . A second condition, the curvature (Wolfe) condition with , additionally rules out steps that are too short; the two together (the Wolfe conditions) are what quasi-Newton methods require to keep their curvature estimates valid.

Pen and paper: one backtracking step

Minimise from along , with . Try : , . The Armijo target is . Since , the full step fails (it overshot the bowl). Backtrack to : , — accepted, and we landed exactly on the minimum. The line search found a stable step without any knowledge of the curvature.

4.2  Trust regions: choose a radius, then the step

A trust region inverts the logic. Instead of choosing a direction then a distance, it fixes a radius within which the local quadratic model is trusted, and solves for the best step inside that ball: After the step, compare the actual decrease in to the decrease the model predicted. If the model was accurate (ratio near ), expand the region; if it was poor, shrink it and retry. The payoff is robustness where line search struggles: when the curvature is indefinite (a saddle, common in non-convex problems), the trust region still produces a sensible bounded step, whereas a pure Newton direction could shoot off toward the saddle. The Levenberg–Marquardt method of Chapter 7 is, in disguise, a trust-region method — its damping parameter is a Lagrange multiplier for the radius constraint.

Which to use

Rule of thumb: line search with a quasi-Newton direction is the default for smooth unconstrained problems where gradients are cheap and reliable; trust regions are preferred when the model curvature can be indefinite or unreliable, or when you want strong global-convergence guarantees. In large-scale deep learning neither is used in the classical form — evaluating exactly is too expensive and the gradient is noisy — which is exactly why the stochastic methods of Part IV replace them with fixed or scheduled step sizes.

5Newton's method: using curvature

If the local quadratic picture is the right picture, jump straight to the bottom of that quadratic. The result is the fastest convergence any method achieves near a solution — at a price.

Gradient descent uses only the slope and so must guess how far to step. Newton's method uses the curvature too. Take the local quadratic model from Taylor, , and minimise it exactly over . Setting its gradient to zero, , gives the Newton step Where gradient descent takes with a scalar , Newton takes : it replaces the single step size with the full inverse-curvature matrix, which rescales and rotates the step so that one jump lands at the minimum of the local quadratic. If actually is quadratic, that is the true minimum and Newton converges in a single step.

5.1  Quadratic convergence

Near a minimum where , Newton's error obeys : the error squares each step. In digits, the number of correct figures roughly doubles per iteration — from 2 correct digits to 4, to 8, to 16 — so from a decent starting point full double precision arrives in a handful of steps. No first-order method can do this; it is the reward for using second-order information.

Pen and paper: Newton finds a square root

Newton's method for is the familiar root-finder applied to the derivative. To compute , minimise , whose minimum is at . Here and ; one Newton step from is . Then , , , . The correct digits roughly double each step — quadratic convergence, by hand.

5.2  The catches, and the fixes

Pure Newton has three well-known failure modes, each with a standard remedy. It can diverge from a bad start — the local quadratic is only trusted nearby — fixed by a line search on the Newton direction (, the “damped Newton” used in the figure) or by a trust region. It chases saddles: if is indefinite, can point uphill, since Newton solves without caring whether the stationary point is a min, max or saddle — fixed by modifying to be positive definite (add until it is) or using a trust region. It is expensive: forming the Hessian costs storage and solving the linear system costs . For in the thousands this is already heavy; for the billions of parameters in a neural network it is unthinkable. The next two chapters are the two great escapes from this cost — approximate the Hessian cheaply (quasi-Newton), or exploit special structure (Gauss–Newton) — and Part IV returns with the deep-learning answers.

6Quasi-Newton methods: BFGS and L-BFGS

Get most of Newton's speed without ever forming or inverting the Hessian — by building an approximation to it from the gradients you were computing anyway. This is the default workhorse of smooth nonlinear optimisation.

Newton is fast but expensive; gradient descent is cheap but slow. Quasi-Newton methods occupy the sweet spot: they keep a running approximation (or directly its inverse ), updated each step using only gradient differences, and take the step with a line search. No second derivatives are ever computed.

6.1  The secant idea

The key observation is that consecutive gradients already contain curvature information. In one dimension, — a finite difference of the slope. The multivariate generalisation is the secant equation: writing the step and the gradient change , we demand that the new curvature estimate reproduce that change, This is the matrix analogue of “curvature = change in slope / change in position.” It does not determine uniquely (one equation, many matrix unknowns), so quasi-Newton methods add a principle: choose the closest to that satisfies the secant equation and stays symmetric positive definite.

6.2  BFGS

The Broyden–Fletcher–Goldfarb–Shanno (BFGS) update is the overwhelmingly dominant choice. It updates the inverse Hessian directly — so each step needs only matrix–vector products, no solve — with a rank-two correction: As long as the curvature condition holds (guaranteed by a Wolfe line search, Chapter 4), each stays symmetric positive definite, so the direction is always a descent direction. BFGS converges superlinearly — faster than any linear rate, approaching Newton's quadratic speed — at cost per step instead of Newton's , and without a single second derivative.

6.3  L-BFGS: the large-scale version

BFGS stores the full inverse-Hessian approximation — fine for in the hundreds or low thousands, impossible for millions. Limited-memory BFGS (L-BFGS) never forms the matrix at all. Instead it keeps only the last pairs — typically to — and reconstructs the action of on the gradient by a clever two-loop recursion through those stored vectors. Cost and storage drop to , linear in the number of variables. L-BFGS is the standard method for smooth, medium-to-large optimisation where gradients are exact: logistic regression, maximum-likelihood fits, physics-based inverse problems, and classical model calibration all lean on it. Its limitation is the same “exact gradient” assumption as line search — with the noisy gradients of large-scale deep learning its curvature estimates degrade, which is why neural nets are trained by the methods of Part IV, not by L-BFGS.

Pen and paper: the secant equation in 1-D

Take , so and the true curvature is . Step from to : then and . The secant equation gives — it recovers the exact curvature from two gradients, no second derivative taken. In many dimensions the same division becomes the rank-two BFGS update, and one step rarely pins down the whole matrix, but each step injects one more direction's worth of true curvature.

7Gauss–Newton and Levenberg–Marquardt

When the objective is a sum of squared residuals — the single most common shape in curve-fitting, calibration and inverse problems — its special structure hands you a Hessian approximation for free.

A huge fraction of practical optimisation is nonlinear least squares: fit model parameters so that residuals are small, by minimising This covers curve fitting, bundle adjustment in vision, orbit determination, and the forward-model calibration at the heart of many physics pipelines. The least-squares shape has structure the general methods ignore, and exploiting it is the difference between a fit that converges in five steps and one that limps.

7.1  The Gauss–Newton approximation

Let be the Jacobian of the residuals, . Differentiating gives the exact gradient and Hessian The Hessian has two parts: , built only from first derivatives, and a second term weighted by the residuals . The Gauss–Newton method simply drops the second term: This is an outstanding bargain. We get a curvature matrix — and hence near-Newton steps — using only the Jacobian, which we need for the gradient anyway; no second derivatives of the model are ever formed. The approximation is excellent precisely when the fit is good, because then the residuals are small and the dropped term is negligible. (You may recognise as the normal equations: each step solves a linear least-squares problem, the linearised version of the nonlinear one.)

7.2  Levenberg–Marquardt: damping for safety

Gauss–Newton can take reckless steps when is nearly singular (poorly determined parameters) or when you start far from the solution. Levenberg–Marquardt (LM) adds a damping term that interpolates smoothly between Gauss–Newton and gradient descent: When this is Gauss–Newton (fast, trusting the curvature); when is large it becomes a small, safe scaled-gradient step. The algorithm adapts on the fly: if a step reduces the cost, accept it and decrease (trust the model more); if it fails, reject and increase (be more cautious). This is a trust region in disguise — is the multiplier for a constraint on the step length — and it makes LM extraordinarily robust. It is the default behind scipy.optimize.curve_fit and essentially every serious curve-fitter.

Why a physicist should care

The matrix is, up to a noise factor, the Fisher information matrix for a Gaussian measurement model — the very object used for parameter-uncertainty forecasting. Its inverse approximates the covariance of the fitted parameters, so a least-squares fit hands you an error bar as a by-product: . The link between the curvature that optimises and the curvature that quantifies uncertainty is not a coincidence; it is the thread we pull on in the next chapter, and the same thread that connects optimisation to natural gradients in Chapter 13.

8Curvature: Hessian, Gauss–Newton, Fisher

The pivot of the whole note. Three different matrices all play the role of “curvature,” they coincide under clean conditions, and knowing how they relate is what unlocks natural gradients, K-FAC and the modern second-order optimisers — and ties optimisation to uncertainty quantification.

Every second-order method takes a step of the form , where is some notion of curvature. Newton uses the Hessian; Gauss–Newton uses ; natural gradient (next part) uses the Fisher information. These are not three unrelated tricks — they are three views of the same object, and seeing how they line up is the single most clarifying idea in advanced optimisation.

8.1  The three matrices

Hessian
, the true second derivative of the objective. Exact local curvature, but can be indefinite (negative eigenvalues at saddles), and expensive — to store, to invert.
Gauss–Newton
For a loss built from a model passed through a convex criterion, with the model Jacobian. Always positive semidefinite — it is the Hessian with the “residual  model-curvature” term dropped (Chapter 7).
Fisher information
, the covariance of the score of a probabilistic model . It measures how sharply the log-likelihood peaks — how much the data constrain the parameters — and is always positive semidefinite.

8.2  Why they coincide

The three collapse into one under conditions that hold remarkably often. For a probabilistic model, a classical identity says the Fisher information equals the expected Hessian of the negative log-likelihood, so is the (expected) Hessian of the loss when the loss is a negative log-likelihood — which covers least squares (Gaussian likelihood) and cross-entropy (categorical likelihood), i.e. almost all of machine learning. And for those same exponential-family losses, the Gauss–Newton matrix equals the Fisher exactly. So:

The identity worth memorising

For a model trained with a negative-log-likelihood loss from the exponential family (least squares, logistic / softmax cross-entropy), The Gauss–Newton matrix, the Fisher information, and the expected Hessian are the same matrix. This is why “Gauss–Newton,” “natural gradient,” and “generalised Gauss–Newton” describe the same step in the deep-learning literature, and why the Fisher — a quantity about information and uncertainty — turns out to be exactly the curvature you want for optimisation.

This is the thread a physicist has already been pulling. The Fisher matrix used to forecast parameter error bars (Cramér–Rao: ) is identically the curvature that a second-order optimiser needs to precondition its steps. The matrix that tells you how well you can know the parameters is the matrix that tells you how to move them efficiently. One object, two uses.

8.3  Preconditioning: what curvature buys you

Whatever we call it, multiplying the gradient by inverse curvature does one thing geometrically: it undoes the stretch of the problem. An ill-conditioned bowl (large ) becomes round in the rescaled coordinates, so a single step size now suits every direction and the zigzag of Chapter 2 vanishes. This is preconditioning, and it is the unifying view of Newton, Gauss–Newton, natural gradient and the adaptive methods: each is gradient descent in a cleverly rescaled space. The step is steepest descent not in the ordinary Euclidean metric but in the metric defined by .

The practical catch is cost: the exact is as expensive as Newton. The entire art of modern second-order optimisation, which Part IV takes up, is building a cheap approximate — diagonal (Adam), block-Kronecker-factored (K-FAC), or Kronecker-of-moments (Shampoo) — that captures enough of the stretch to help, without the bill.

9Convex optimisation and duality

The part of optimisation where we can promise a global optimum, certify it, and often solve fast. Even when your real problem is non-convex, convex thinking supplies the lower bounds and the local models.

Chapter 1 drew the dividing line: for a convex objective, every local minimum is global, so there is nowhere bad to get stuck. This chapter gives the two further gifts convexity brings — a rich toolbox of problem classes that solvers handle to machine precision, and duality, a way to certify that a candidate solution is optimal.

9.1  The convex toolbox

A surprising amount of applied modelling can be cast in a handful of convex forms, each with mature, reliable solvers. Linear programs (linear objective, linear constraints) run logistics and planning. Quadratic programs (convex quadratic objective, linear constraints) are the engine of mean–variance portfolio optimisation and support-vector machines. Second-order cone and semidefinite programs reach robust optimisation, control, and relaxations of hard combinatorial problems. The practical skill is recognising — or massaging — a problem into one of these classes, because once it is in, global optimality is essentially guaranteed. Operations like nonnegative combinations, pointwise maxima, and composition with affine maps preserve convexity, which is how you check that a model you have built stays in the tractable world.

9.2  Duality: a certificate of optimality

Every minimisation (the primal) has a shadow problem, the dual, built by folding the constraints into the objective with Lagrange multipliers and then minimising out the original variables. The dual is always a maximisation, and it has a beautiful property: weak duality says every dual value is a lower bound on every primal value. So any feasible dual point certifies that the primal optimum is no smaller than some number — a guarantee you could never get from the primal alone, where you only ever have upper bounds (the best point found so far).

The gap between the best primal and best dual values is the duality gap. Strong duality — the gap is zero — holds for essentially all convex problems with a feasible interior (Slater's condition). When it holds, primal and dual optima coincide, and a matching primal–dual pair is a proof of optimality: you can stop and know you are done. This certificate is the practical reason convex solvers can report rigorous accuracy, and duality gaps are the standard stopping criterion inside interior-point methods. In machine learning the same idea surfaces as the dual form of the SVM (where the multipliers become the support vectors) and as the lower bounds that make the ELBO work in variational inference — duality is not an abstraction, it is how you know when to stop.

Non-convex problems borrow convex tools

Even when the real objective is non-convex — a neural network, say — convexity still earns its keep. Every trust-region or Newton step solves a convex quadratic model of the local landscape. Many hard problems are tackled by a convex relaxation that gives a lower bound and a starting point. And the loss as a function of the model's outputs is usually convex even when it is wildly non-convex in the parameters — the fact that makes the Gauss–Newton matrix of Chapter 8 positive semidefinite. The convex world is the ground the non-convex methods stand on.

10Constrained optimisation: Lagrange and KKT

Most real problems come with limits — budgets, physical laws, bounds. The method of Lagrange multipliers, generalised to inequalities as the KKT conditions, turns a constrained problem into a set of equations in the variables and a few multipliers.

We now want to minimise subject to equality constraints and inequality constraints . The feasible set is carved out by these, and the minimum we seek lives on or inside its boundary. The central idea is to stop treating the constraints as a wall and instead price them: each constraint gets a multiplier, and at the optimum the objective's pull is exactly balanced by the constraints' prices.

10.1  Equality constraints: Lagrange multipliers

For a single equality , form the Lagrangian Setting gives : at the constrained optimum, the gradient of the objective is parallel to the gradient of the constraint. Geometrically (the right panel of the previous chapter) a cost contour is tangent to the constraint surface — if it crossed instead of touched, you could slide along the constraint to a lower contour. The multiplier measures the sensitivity: it is the rate at which the optimal value would change if you relaxed the constraint, the “shadow price” of that constraint. Setting just restores , so the stationary points of solve the constrained problem.

Pen and paper: the largest rectangle on a budget

Maximise area subject to a perimeter budget . Lagrangian: . Stationarity: and , so — the optimum is a square, . The multiplier is : it says the optimal area grows at rate per unit of extra perimeter — the shadow price of the budget. One Lagrangian delivered both the solution and its sensitivity.

10.2  Inequalities: the KKT conditions

Inequality constraints add one idea: a constraint is either active (tight, , pushing on the solution) or inactive (slack, , irrelevant locally). The Karush–Kuhn–Tucker (KKT) conditions package this. With multipliers for the inequalities and for the equalities, a point is a candidate optimum when:

Stationarity
— forces balance between objective and active constraints.
Primal feasibility
, — the point obeys the constraints.
Dual feasibility
— inequality prices only push inward, never pull.
Complementary slackness
— the crucial one: either a constraint is active () or its price is zero (). Slack constraints exert no force.

For convex problems the KKT conditions are not just necessary but sufficient — any point satisfying them is a global optimum — which is what makes them the backbone of convex solvers. Complementary slackness is the combinatorial heart of the matter: solving a constrained problem is, in part, discovering which constraints are active. Interior-point methods do this smoothly by approaching the boundary from inside; active-set methods do it by guessing and correcting the active set.

Where this shows up

The KKT conditions are everywhere once you look: the support vectors of an SVM are exactly the training points with active margin constraints (non-zero ); the water-filling solution in information theory is KKT on a power budget; mean–variance portfolios with no-short-selling bounds are a KKT system; and the dual variables are precisely the Lagrange multipliers that priced the constraints. Learning to read a problem as “which constraints bind, and what are they worth” is one of the most transferable skills in all of optimisation.

11Stochastic gradient descent

When the objective is an average over millions of data points, computing the exact gradient once is wasteful. Estimate it from a small random sample and step anyway. This one change is what makes training modern models possible.

Machine-learning objectives are averages over data: , with the loss on example and in the millions or billions. The exact gradient requires a full pass over the data for a single step — absurd when a model needs hundreds of thousands of steps. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) estimates the gradient from a random minibatch of size : Each is an unbiased estimate of the true gradient — right on average — but noisy. The bet, which pays off spectacularly, is that many cheap noisy steps beat a few expensive exact ones.

11.1  The bias–variance of a step

Because , SGD descends in expectation. The variance of scales like : a batch of 32 has roughly less gradient noise than a single example, and a full batch () has none. This is the fundamental trade-off of the method — larger batches give cleaner gradients and steadier progress but cost proportionally more per step, so there is an efficient batch size, not simply “bigger is better.”

11.2  The learning-rate schedule

With noisy gradients a constant step size cannot converge to a point: near the minimum the true gradient is tiny but the noise is not, so the iterates bounce around in a “noise ball” whose radius is set by . To actually converge you must shrink the step. The classical Robbins–Monro conditions make this precise: a schedule guarantees convergence if (steps still add up to cover any distance) and (the accumulated noise is finite). The canonical satisfies both. In deep learning the schedules are more elaborate — warmup then cosine decay is standard — but the principle is the one in the figure: decay the step to settle the noise.

Pen and paper: why the noise ball has a floor

Model SGD near the minimum of a 1-D quadratic with gradient noise of variance : , . At steady state the variance satisfies , giving The residual variance is proportional to : halving the learning rate halves the noise-ball size, and only reaches the exact minimum — which is precisely why schedules decay. It also shows the trade: a bigger moves faster early but settles coarser.

A last point of intuition: SGD's noise is not purely a nuisance. In the non-convex landscapes of deep learning it helps the iterate escape sharp local minima and saddles, and there is good evidence it biases training toward flatter minima that generalise better. The same randomness that forces a decaying schedule is part of why SGD-trained networks work as well as they do — a theme we return to in Chapter 15.

12Adaptive methods: AdaGrad, RMSProp, Adam

Give every parameter its own learning rate, set automatically from the history of its gradients. This cheap, diagonal form of preconditioning is what actually trains most deep networks.

Chapter 8 showed that the right cure for ill-conditioning is to rescale each direction by its curvature — but the full curvature matrix is far too expensive for a large network. The adaptive family makes the cheapest useful approximation: a diagonal preconditioner, one scalar per parameter, estimated from the gradients themselves. It is Chapter 8's preconditioning idea on a shoestring budget, and it works.

12.1  AdaGrad and RMSProp

AdaGrad gives each coordinate a step size inversely proportional to the root of its accumulated squared gradients: (all operations elementwise). Coordinates that have seen large or frequent gradients get small steps; rarely active ones get large steps — a boon for sparse features. Its flaw is that only ever grows, so the effective learning rate decays monotonically to zero and learning can stall. RMSProp fixes this by replacing the running sum with an exponentially-weighted moving average, which forgets old gradients: Now tracks the recent gradient scale, so the per-coordinate step adapts to the current part of the landscape instead of decaying forever.

12.2  Adam = momentum + RMSProp

Adam, the default optimiser for most of deep learning, combines the two ideas of this note's first half: a momentum-style running mean of the gradient (first moment ) and an RMSProp-style running mean of its square (second moment ), with a bias correction so the early-iteration averages are not shrunk toward zero: The numerator is momentum (direction, denoised); the denominator is the per-coordinate rescaling (curvature proxy). Typical defaults , , work across a huge range of problems with little tuning — the reason Adam is the field's workhorse. AdamW, the version used in practice, additionally decouples weight decay from the gradient step, which fixes a subtle interaction that plain Adam gets wrong and matters a lot for generalisation.

The honest limitation

A diagonal preconditioner only rescales the coordinate axes; it cannot fix correlations between parameters — the off-diagonal curvature, the rotation of the bowl. When the ill-conditioning is aligned with the axes (as in the figure) Adam captures it; when it comes from strong parameter correlations, a diagonal method leaves most of the stretch in place. Closing that gap — capturing the off-diagonal curvature cheaply — is exactly what natural gradient and the Kronecker-factored methods of the next two chapters set out to do. Adam is first-order per-coordinate scaling; K-FAC and Shampoo are its structured second-order successors.

13Natural gradient and K-FAC

The steepest-descent direction depends on how you measure distance. Measuring it by the Fisher information — distance in distribution space, not parameter space — gives the natural gradient, the principled second-order method for probabilistic models, and K-FAC makes it affordable.

Ordinary gradient descent has a hidden arbitrariness. The gradient is the steepest-descent direction only with respect to the Euclidean distance in parameter space — but that distance is an accident of how we happened to parameterise the model. Rescale a parameter, or switch from standard deviation to variance, and the Euclidean gradient points somewhere different, even though the model is the same. For a probabilistic model this is clearly wrong: what should matter is how much the model's predictions change, not how much its arbitrary coordinates do.

13.1  Distance in distribution space

The fix is to measure distance by how much the model's output distribution changes — the Kullback–Leibler divergence between and . Expanding the KL to second order, its local metric is exactly the Fisher information: Steepest descent in this metric — the direction that most reduces the loss per unit of change in the output distribution — is the natural gradient: It is preconditioning (Chapter 8) with the Fisher as the curvature, and it is invariant to reparameterisation: rescale the parameters and the natural-gradient step lands in the same place in distribution space. Because for likelihood losses (Chapter 8), natural gradient is a Gauss–Newton / approximate-Newton method — the same step, reached from the geometry of probability rather than the calculus of the loss surface.

The physicist's shortcut

If you have ever drawn Fisher-matrix forecast ellipses — the confidence contours of a parameter estimate — you already have the natural gradient's geometry in your hands. Those ellipses are the distribution-space metric. The natural gradient simply steps along , i.e. it moves “one unit of confidence ellipse” at a time rather than one unit of parameter. The matrix you built to forecast how well an experiment could measure its parameters is the matrix that tells a model how to learn them efficiently. This is the single cleanest bridge from a forecasting-and-inference background into modern optimisation.

13.2  K-FAC: making it affordable

The obstacle is familiar: for a real network is enormous, and is hopeless to form directly. K-FAC (Kronecker-Factored Approximate Curvature) is the breakthrough that made natural gradient practical for deep nets. Its insight is that, for a single layer, the Fisher block has approximately a Kronecker-product structure: where is the (small) covariance of that layer's inputs and the covariance of the back-propagated gradients at its outputs. The Kronecker identity then means you only ever invert the two small factors, never the giant block: a layer with inputs and outputs replaces an inverse with an and an one. K-FAC thus captures the off-diagonal curvature within each layer — the correlations Adam's diagonal cannot see — at a cost only a few times a gradient step, and on many problems it reaches a target loss in noticeably fewer steps than Adam. It is the direct ancestor of the methods in the next chapter.

14Modern second-order methods: Shampoo and SOAP

The current frontier of training optimisers. They take K-FAC's Kronecker-factored curvature idea, build it from the optimiser's own running statistics, and have begun to beat Adam on the largest models — the family a research role in optimisation now lives in.

Adam gave every parameter its own learning rate from a diagonal estimate; K-FAC captured within-layer correlations through a Kronecker factorisation of the Fisher. The newest methods push this structured second-order idea into something practical at the scale of today's large models, and they are an active, fast-moving research area rather than settled textbook material.

14.1  Shampoo

Shampoo preconditions the gradient of each weight matrix with a Kronecker product of two statistics it accumulates itself, rather than from an explicit Fisher estimate. For a weight matrix with gradient , it maintains left and right preconditioners from the running sums and takes the step The matrix fourth-roots and precondition the gradient's rows and columns separately — a full-matrix preconditioner for each layer, factored so the two factors stay small enough to handle. It is the same “Kronecker-factored curvature” spirit as K-FAC, but assembled from the gradient second moments the optimiser already tracks (closer to Adam's machinery) rather than from input/output covariances. Distributed and low-rank variants have made Shampoo practical at large scale, where it has delivered real wall-clock speed-ups over Adam.

14.2  SOAP

SOAP (ShampoO with Adam in the Preconditioner's eigenbasis) is a recent refinement that ties the two families together with a clean idea: run plain Adam, but in the rotating eigenbasis that Shampoo's preconditioner defines. Shampoo supplies which directions matter (the eigenvectors of its Kronecker factors, updated slowly); Adam supplies a cheap, well-understood per-coordinate step within that rotated frame. The result keeps Shampoo's ability to see off-diagonal, full-matrix curvature while inheriting Adam's robustness and reducing how often the expensive matrix operations must run, and it has shown strong results on large language-model training.

The through-line, in one sentence

Every optimiser in Part IV is “gradient descent, preconditioned by an ever-better and ever-cheaper approximation of the curvature”: SGD uses the identity (no preconditioner), Adam a diagonal, K-FAC a Kronecker-factored Fisher, and Shampoo/SOAP a Kronecker-factored full-matrix preconditioner from the gradient's own moments. The research question of the day is the same one that runs through this whole note — how much curvature can you afford to use? — now asked at the scale of frontier models.

Where the research actually is

Two caveats keep this honest. First, Adam/AdamW remains an extremely strong, well-tuned baseline, and second-order methods win only when their per-step overhead and extra memory are paid back by enough reduction in step count — which depends on model, batch size and hardware. Second, the named methods change year to year (Lion, Sophia, Muon and others sit alongside Shampoo and SOAP); what does not change is the underlying grammar — momentum, variance/curvature estimation, and preconditioning — which is why this note spends its effort there. A practitioner who understands Chapters 8, 12 and 13 can read a new optimiser paper and place it immediately.

15Training large models in practice

The craft around the optimiser — initialisation, batch size, warmup and schedules, regularisation, and distributing the work across many GPUs — that decides whether a billion-parameter model trains at all.

The optimiser is one component of training; the engineering around it is the rest. None of it changes the mathematics of the previous chapters, but all of it changes whether that mathematics gets a chance to work. This chapter collects the practical ideas that matter most, each a direct consequence of something already established.

15.1  Initialisation and normalisation

Where you start sets the curvature you begin in. Initialise weights too large and activations (and gradients) explode through the layers; too small and they vanish — either way the loss surface near the start is pathologically conditioned. The standard schemes (Xavier/Glorot, He) scale the initial weights by the layer width precisely to keep the variance of activations and gradients roughly constant across depth. Normalisation layers (batch, layer, RMS norm) go further, actively rescaling activations during training; a large part of their benefit is that they smooth and better-condition the loss landscape, so the optimiser sees a rounder bowl. Both are conditioning fixes (Chapter 2) applied before and during the run rather than inside the optimiser.

15.2  Batch size, warmup, and schedules

Batch size trades gradient noise against cost (Chapter 11), but it also interacts with the learning rate. A useful rule of thumb is linear scaling: if you multiply the batch size by , multiply the learning rate by about too, since a cleaner gradient can bear a bigger step — valid until the step grows large enough to break the local-quadratic assumption, where it fails. That failure is why warmup is standard: start with a tiny learning rate and ramp up over the first few thousand steps, because early in training the curvature estimates (Adam's , say) are unreliable and a large step can diverge. After warmup, a decaying schedule — cosine is the common choice — settles the noise ball as Chapter 11 requires. The modern recipe, warmup-then-cosine with AdamW, is every principle in Part IV stacked together.

Regularisation is optimisation too

Weight decay, early stopping and dropout all reshape what is being optimised. Weight decay adds an penalty that lifts the loss away from large-norm solutions — and, as noted in Chapter 12, must be decoupled from the adaptive step (AdamW) to act as intended. Early stopping halts before the optimiser fits the noise — it is a form of implicit regularisation, limiting how far into the landscape you travel. These are not separate from optimisation; they change the objective or the trajectory, and are best understood in the same language.

15.3  Distributed training

Once a model or its data will not fit on one device, the optimiser's work is split across many — and the splitting is itself an engineering discipline. Data parallelism replicates the model on each GPU, each processing a different slice of the batch; the gradients are averaged across devices (an all-reduce) before the step, so every replica stays in sync — mathematically identical to one large-batch SGD step. When the model itself is too big, sharded schemes (ZeRO / FSDP) split the parameters, gradients and optimiser state across devices so no single GPU holds the whole model, gathering each shard just in time; tensor and pipeline parallelism split individual layers or stages across devices. The optimiser mathematics is unchanged — it is still Adam or Shampoo on an averaged gradient — but communication becomes the bottleneck, and overlapping it with computation, reducing its volume, and tolerating stragglers is where the real work goes. (This is the stack — DDP, FSDP, DeepSpeed — worth a hands-on project for anyone moving toward large-scale ML engineering.)

Why non-convex training works anyway

A reasonable worry hangs over all of this: neural-network losses are wildly non-convex, so why does any of it converge to something good? The empirical answer, now well supported, is that in very high dimensions the troublesome critical points are overwhelmingly saddles, not bad local minima, and the large number of near-equivalent good minima means almost any of them is fine. SGD's noise (Chapter 11) helps slide off saddles and appears to favour flat, generalising minima. The theory is still catching up to the practice, but the working picture is that high dimension is a help, not a hindrance — there are too many escape routes for a method to stay stuck.

16Global and derivative-free optimisation

When you cannot differentiate, when each evaluation is expensive, or when the landscape is riddled with local minima, the gradient-based toolkit runs out. These methods trade derivative information for exploration — and Bayesian optimisation turns each evaluation into a decision.

Everything so far assumed a smooth objective with a computable gradient and was content to find a local minimum. Three situations break those assumptions: the objective is a black box with no gradient (a simulation, a physical experiment, someone else's code); each evaluation is very expensive (train a model, run a wind-tunnel test), so you get only tens or hundreds of them; or the landscape has many local minima and you genuinely need the global one. The methods here address those cases, at the cost of the fast convergence that gradients buy.

16.1  Local minima and the need to explore

A gradient method is relentlessly local: from a given start it rolls to the nearest basin and stops, with no way to know a deeper valley lies elsewhere. Simulated annealing escapes this by sometimes accepting uphill moves, with a probability borrowed from statistical physics: at high “temperature” the search wanders freely over barriers; as is slowly lowered, the moves become pickier and the search settles into — with luck — the global basin. The willingness to go uphill is exactly what a gradient method lacks.

Evolutionary and population methods (genetic algorithms, CMA-ES, particle swarm) take a different route to the same goal: keep a population of candidates and improve it by mutation, recombination and selection, with no gradient at all. CMA-ES in particular adapts a full covariance of its sampling distribution — learning the local curvature from the spread of good samples — and is a genuinely strong black-box optimiser in moderate dimensions. These methods are robust and parallelise trivially, but need many evaluations, so they suit cheap-to-evaluate, non-differentiable objectives.

16.2  Bayesian optimisation: when every evaluation is precious

When each evaluation is expensive — the defining case being hyperparameter tuning, where one “evaluation” is training a whole model — you cannot afford the thousands of samples a population method wants. Bayesian optimisation makes each evaluation a deliberate decision. It fits a probabilistic surrogate — usually a Gaussian process — to the evaluations so far, giving both a predicted value and a calibrated uncertainty everywhere, and then chooses the next point to evaluate by maximising an acquisition function that balances exploitation (sample where the surrogate predicts a good value) against exploration (sample where it is uncertain). Expected Improvement is the classic choice: it scores each candidate by how much it is expected to beat the best value seen, integrating over the surrogate's uncertainty.

The uncertainty is the point

Bayesian optimisation is where this note's optimisation thread meets the inference thread: the whole method runs on a calibrated posterior over the objective, and it works only as well as that uncertainty is honest. Over-confident error bars and it stops exploring too soon, missing the global minimum; under-confident and it wastes expensive evaluations. The same calibration that matters for trustworthy prediction is what makes the acquisition function point in the right direction — a reminder that good optimisation of expensive functions is a problem in uncertainty quantification.

17The whole subject on one page

Every method in this note is one of four ideas — follow the slope, use the curvature, estimate the gradient cheaply, rescale the space — combined and sharpened for a setting. Here they are, side by side.

It is worth stepping back to see how little is really going on. The table below is the note in miniature: each row is a method, and the columns say what gradient it uses, what curvature (if any), and what it costs. Read top to bottom and you watch the same two levers — how much gradient you can afford, how much curvature you can afford — being pushed in every direction.

The four ideas, once more

1. Follow the slope. Gradient descent; the irreducible core.
2. Use the curvature. Newton, quasi-Newton, Gauss–Newton — the second derivative tells you how far to step and in what shape, buying superlinear or quadratic convergence.
3. Estimate the gradient cheaply. SGD — a noisy sample of the gradient makes enormous problems tractable, at the price of a learning-rate schedule to settle the noise.
4. Rescale the space. Preconditioning — from Adam's diagonal to natural gradient's Fisher to Shampoo's Kronecker factors — undo the problem's stretch so a single step size suits every direction. This is the idea the research frontier keeps refining.

The thread that runs through all four, and through this note, is curvature — and the quiet discovery, made explicit in Chapter 8, that the curvature which optimises (the Hessian) and the curvature which quantifies uncertainty (the Fisher information) are, for the models we actually use, the same matrix. The object that tells you how well you can know your parameters is the object that tells you how to move them. Hold onto that, and every optimiser from least squares to the latest training method is a variation on one theme: estimate the curvature as well as you can afford to, and step accordingly.

18Appendix — the algorithms, in code

Every figure in this note came from the equations in it. These are the load-bearing lines, so you can reproduce and play. All elementwise operations use NumPy broadcasting.

A.1  Gradient descent, momentum, Nesterov (Ch. 2–3)

import numpy as np

def gradient_descent(grad, x0, lr, n):
    x = np.array(x0, float)
    for _ in range(n):
        x = x - lr*grad(x)
    return x

def momentum(grad, x0, lr, beta, n, nesterov=False):
    x = np.array(x0, float); v = np.zeros_like(x)
    for _ in range(n):
        g = grad(x + beta*v) if nesterov else grad(x)   # look-ahead if Nesterov
        v = beta*v - lr*g
        x = x + v
    return x

A.2  Backtracking line search (Ch. 4)

def backtracking(f, grad, x, d, alpha=1.0, c1=1e-4, rho=0.5):
    fx = f(x); gTd = grad(x) @ d                 # directional derivative
    while f(x + alpha*d) > fx + c1*alpha*gTd:    # Armijo sufficient-decrease
        alpha *= rho
    return alpha

A.3  Damped Newton (Ch. 5)

def newton(grad, hess, x0, n, reg=1e-6):
    x = np.array(x0, float)
    for _ in range(n):
        g = grad(x); H = hess(x)
        step = np.linalg.solve(H + reg*np.eye(len(x)), g)   # solve H d = g
        a = 1.0                                             # backtrack on the Newton direction
        while f(x - a*step) > f(x) - 1e-4*a*(g @ step) and a > 1e-4:
            a *= 0.5
        x = x - a*step
    return x

A.4  BFGS inverse-Hessian update (Ch. 6)

def bfgs_step(Hinv, s, y):                       # s = x_{k+1}-x_k,  y = grad diff
    rho = 1.0/(y @ s)
    I = np.eye(len(s))
    V = I - rho*np.outer(s, y)
    return V @ Hinv @ V.T + rho*np.outer(s, s)   # rank-two update, stays SPD if y@s>0

A.5  Gauss–Newton / Levenberg–Marquardt (Ch. 7)

def levenberg_marquardt(resid, jac, p0, n, lam=1e-2):
    p = np.array(p0, float); cost = 0.5*np.sum(resid(p)**2)
    for _ in range(n):
        J = jac(p); r = resid(p)
        A = J.T @ J; g = J.T @ r
        step = np.linalg.solve(A + lam*np.diag(np.diag(A)), g)   # damped normal equations
        if 0.5*np.sum(resid(p-step)**2) < cost:                  # step helped
            p = p - step; cost = 0.5*np.sum(resid(p)**2); lam *= 0.5   # trust more
        else:
            lam *= 3.0                                           # be more cautious
    return p

A.6  SGD with a decaying schedule (Ch. 11)

def sgd(grad_i, N, w0, n, lr0=0.2, decay=0.01, batch=1):
    w = np.array(w0, float); rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    for k in range(n):
        idx = rng.integers(0, N, batch)          # random minibatch
        g = grad_i(w, idx)                        # unbiased gradient estimate
        lr = lr0/(1 + decay*k)                    # Robbins-Monro schedule
        w = w - lr*g
    return w

A.7  Adam (Ch. 12)

def adam(grad, w0, n, lr=1e-3, b1=0.9, b2=0.999, eps=1e-8):
    w = np.array(w0, float); m = np.zeros_like(w); s = np.zeros_like(w)
    for k in range(1, n+1):
        g = grad(w)
        m = b1*m + (1-b1)*g                       # 1st moment (momentum)
        s = b2*s + (1-b2)*g*g                     # 2nd moment (per-coord variance)
        mh = m/(1-b1**k); sh = s/(1-b2**k)        # bias correction
        w = w - lr*mh/(np.sqrt(sh) + eps)
    return w

A.8  Natural gradient, and Shampoo's preconditioned step (Ch. 13–14)

def natural_gradient_step(grad, fisher, w, lr):
    g = grad(w); F = fisher(w)
    return w - lr*np.linalg.solve(F, g)           # step along F^{-1} grad

def shampoo_step(W, G, L, R, lr, eps=1e-6):       # W,G are weight & gradient MATRICES
    L = L + G @ G.T; R = R + G.T @ G              # accumulate left/right statistics
    Lh = fractional_matrix_power(L + eps*np.eye(L.shape[0]), -0.25)
    Rh = fractional_matrix_power(R + eps*np.eye(R.shape[0]), -0.25)
    return W - lr*(Lh @ G @ Rh), L, R             # Kronecker-factored preconditioning

A.9  Bayesian optimisation with Expected Improvement (Ch. 16)

from scipy.stats import norm
def expected_improvement(mu, sd, best):
    imp = best - mu                               # improvement over best-so-far (minimising)
    Z = np.divide(imp, sd, out=np.zeros_like(mu), where=sd>0)
    ei = imp*norm.cdf(Z) + sd*norm.pdf(Z)         # exploit + explore
    ei[sd <= 0] = 0.0
    return ei                                     # next evaluation = argmax EI
